body:
The two principal motions of Earth

Earth is continuously moving in space. Its two principal motions are rotation and revolution. These motions occur simultaneously but produce different geographical effects.

  • Rotation: The spinning of Earth about its own axis. It produces the regular succession of day and night.
  • Revolution: The movement of Earth around the Sun along its orbit. Together with Earth's axial tilt, it produces the annual cycle of seasons.

Earth's axis and its inclination

Earth's axis is an imaginary line passing through its centre and joining the North Pole and the South Pole. Earth rotates around this line.

The plane containing Earth's orbit around the Sun is called the orbital plane or the plane of the ecliptic. Earth's rotational axis is not perpendicular to this plane.

  • Earth's axis is inclined at approximately 66.5° to its orbital plane.
  • Earth's axis is tilted approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane.
  • Earth's equatorial plane is inclined approximately 23.5° to its orbital plane.

These angles describe the same axial inclination from different reference lines or planes. The axial tilt is also known as the obliquity of the ecliptic.

Direction and duration of rotation

Earth rotates from west to east. Viewed from above the North Pole, its rotation is anticlockwise. Viewed from above the South Pole, it is clockwise.

Because Earth rotates eastward, the Sun and most stars appear to move westward across the sky. The apparent daily movement of the Sun is therefore opposite to Earth's actual direction of rotation.

MeasurementDurationReference
Sidereal dayAbout 23 hours 56 minutes 4 secondsDistant stars
Mean solar day24 hoursMean apparent motion of the Sun

A sidereal day measures one complete rotation relative to distant stars. A solar day measures the interval between successive passages of the Sun across the same local meridian. As Earth advances along its orbit while rotating, it must turn slightly more than 360° to bring the Sun back to approximately the same position in the local sky.

How rotation produces day and night

At any given moment, approximately half of Earth's surface faces the Sun and receives sunlight. The opposite half faces away from the Sun and remains dark.

The imaginary boundary separating the illuminated and dark portions of Earth is called the circle of illumination, also known as the terminator.

As Earth rotates, a location moves from the dark portion into the illuminated portion, producing sunrise. Later, it moves from the illuminated portion into darkness, producing sunset.

Other geographical effects of rotation

  • Earth's mean angular rotation corresponds to approximately 15° per hour, producing a local solar time difference of about 4 minutes for every 1° of longitude.
  • Places farther east generally experience local solar noon earlier than places farther west.
  • Rotation contributes to Earth's equatorial bulge and slight flattening at the poles.
  • The rotational linear speed is greatest at the Equator and decreases towards the poles.

Although Earth's angular speed is approximately the same at all latitudes, places near the Equator travel around larger circles during each rotation than places near the poles.

Prelims focus

  • Earth rotates from west to east.
  • A mean solar day lasts 24 hours.
  • A sidereal day lasts approximately 23 hours 56 minutes.
  • Earth's axis makes an angle of 66.5° with its orbital plane.
  • The circle of illumination separates daylight from darkness.
  • Trap: The axial tilt of 23.5° is measured from the perpendicular to the orbital plane, not from the orbital plane itself.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapters 2 and 3, pp. 10-15 and 18-21; NASA, Basics of Space Flight, Chapter 2, Reference Systems, section on Earth's Rotation, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Earth's Rotation: Axis, Day and Night

body:
Planetary motions

All 8 planets of the Solar System revolve around the Sun and rotate about their own axes. However, their rotational directions, rotational periods, orbital periods and axial inclinations differ considerably.

In increasing order of distance from the Sun, the planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Prograde and retrograde rotation

The planets revolve around the Sun in the same general direction. Viewed from above the northern side of the Solar System's orbital plane, their revolution is anticlockwise.

Most planets also rotate in the same general direction as their revolution. This is known as prograde rotation.

Rotation in the direction opposite to the general direction of planetary revolution is called retrograde rotation. Venus and Uranus are the 2 planets with retrograde axial rotation.

  • Venus: Rotates extremely slowly in the reverse direction compared with Earth. Its axial inclination is approximately 177.4°.
  • Uranus: Has an axial inclination of approximately 97.8°. Its rotational axis lies almost parallel to its orbital plane, making it appear to roll on its side while revolving around the Sun.

Comparison of planetary periods

A planet's rotation period measures the time required to complete one spin around its axis. Its revolution period measures the time required to complete one orbit around the Sun.

PlanetRotation periodRevolution periodRotation
Mercury58.6 days88 daysPrograde
Venus243 days225 daysRetrograde
Earth23.9 hours365.25 daysPrograde
Mars24.6 hours687 daysPrograde
Jupiter9.9 hours11.9 yearsPrograde
Saturn10.7 hours29.4 yearsPrograde
Uranus17.2 hours84.0 yearsRetrograde
Neptune16.1 hours164.8 yearsPrograde

These are approximate periods expressed in Earth-based units. The rotation periods of the giant planets are representative values because their different atmospheric regions do not all rotate at exactly the same speed.

Important planetary comparisons

  • Fastest axial rotation: Jupiter completes one rotation in less than 10 hours.
  • Slowest axial rotation: Venus takes approximately 243 Earth days to complete one rotation.
  • Shortest revolution period: Mercury completes one orbit around the Sun in approximately 88 Earth days.
  • Longest revolution period: Neptune takes approximately 165 Earth years to complete one orbit.
  • Rotation closest to Earth's duration: Mars completes one rotation in approximately 24.6 hours.

Rotation period and solar day are different

The term day can refer either to a planet's axial rotation period or to the interval between successive solar noons. These durations are not necessarily equal.

Venus is particularly important because its rotation period of approximately 243 Earth days is longer than its revolution period of approximately 225 Earth days. However, its solar day is approximately 117 Earth days because it rotates in the retrograde direction.

On Venus, the Sun generally rises in the west and sets in the east, opposite to the familiar pattern on Earth.

Mercury completes one axial rotation in approximately 59 Earth days, but its solar day lasts approximately 176 Earth days. This is equal to approximately 2 Mercury years.

Distinguish rotation from revolution

Jupiter is the fastest rotating planet, whereas Mercury has the shortest revolution period around the Sun. The planet with the shortest year does not necessarily have the shortest day.

Prelims focus

  • Venus and Uranus exhibit retrograde rotation.
  • Jupiter has the shortest axial rotation period.
  • Venus has the longest axial rotation period.
  • Mercury has the shortest orbital period.
  • Neptune has the longest orbital period.
  • Trap: Venus's rotation period exceeds its year, but its solar day does not.

[References: NCERT, Class 8, Science, 2018-19, Chapter 17, Stars and the Solar System, pp. 225-231 and Table 17.1, p. 237; NASA NSSDCA, Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric, updated 13 November 2026, reference values as of 26 November 2026; NASA, Venus Facts, Mercury Facts and Uranus Facts, sections on Orbit and Rotation, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Rotation and Revolution of the Eight Planets

body:
Earth's annual motion around the Sun

The movement of Earth around the Sun is called revolution. Earth revolves in an anticlockwise direction when viewed from above the northern side of its orbital plane.

Earth follows an elliptical orbit that is nearly circular. The Sun occupies one of the 2 focal points of this ellipse rather than its exact geometrical centre.

The average Earth-Sun distance is approximately 149.6 million km. Earth's average orbital speed is approximately 29.8 km per second.

Throughout one annual revolution, Earth's rotational axis maintains approximately the same inclination and orientation in space. This property is essential for understanding the seasonal cycle.

Revolution and the calendar year

Earth takes approximately 365.25 days to complete one revolution around the Sun. However, the ordinary civil calendar year contains only 365 days.

The annual cycle of seasons, known as the tropical year, lasts approximately 365.2422 days. Without calendar adjustments, the dates of the seasons would gradually shift.

A leap year contains 366 days, with the additional day inserted as 29 February.

Gregorian calendar rules

  • A year divisible by 4 is normally a leap year.
  • A century year divisible by 100 is not normally a leap year.
  • A century year is a leap year if it is also divisible by 400.

For example, 2000 and 2024 are leap years. The years 1900 and 2100 are not leap years.

Perihelion and aphelion

Because Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, its distance from the Sun changes during the year.

Perihelion is the position in Earth's orbit at which Earth is nearest to the Sun. Aphelion is the position at which Earth is farthest from the Sun.

FeaturePerihelionAphelion
Usual occurrenceEarly JanuaryEarly July
Conventional textbook date3 January4 July
Approximate distance147 million km152 million km
Orbital speedGreatestLowest
Northern Hemisphere seasonWinterSummer

The exact dates of perihelion and aphelion vary slightly from year to year. The dates 3 January and 4 July are conventional approximate dates rather than fixed annual dates.

Variation in orbital speed and solar energy

Earth moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther away. Consequently, its orbital speed is greatest at perihelion and lowest at aphelion.

Earth also receives more intense incoming solar radiation at perihelion than at aphelion. The difference in incoming solar radiation at the top of the atmosphere between these positions is approximately 7%.

However, this variation does not determine which hemisphere experiences summer or winter. The Northern Hemisphere experiences winter when Earth is near perihelion and summer when Earth is near aphelion. This demonstrates the greater importance of axial inclination in producing seasons.

Related orbital terms

Perihelion and aphelion describe distances from the Sun. Corresponding terms for an object orbiting Earth are perigee, its nearest orbital point to Earth, and apogee, its farthest orbital point from Earth. These terms are particularly useful when discussing the Moon's apparent size during eclipses.

Prelims focus

  • Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical.
  • A leap year contains 366 days.
  • Perihelion occurs in early January at approximately 147 million km.
  • Aphelion occurs in early July at approximately 152 million km.
  • Earth moves fastest at perihelion.
  • Trap: Northern Hemisphere summer does not occur because Earth is nearest to the Sun.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapter 3, pp. 19-20; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, 2024-25 online reprint, Chapter 8, pp. 67-68, consulted 26 November 2026, used in place of the unreadable project copy; US Naval Observatory, The Seasons and the Earth's Orbit and Leap Years; NASA NSSDCA, Planetary Fact Sheet - Metric, updated 13 November 2026; NASA, Daily Moon Guide, distance terminology; online references consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Orbital distance is not the principal cause of seasons.

title: Earth's Revolution, Leap Year, Perihelion and Aphelion

body:
The astronomical cause of seasons

The regular annual change between spring, summer, autumn and winter occurs primarily because of Earth's axial inclination and its revolution around the Sun.

Earth's axis is tilted approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane. As Earth revolves around the Sun, this axis continues to point in approximately the same direction in space.

Consequently, the Northern Hemisphere is inclined towards the Sun during one part of the year, while the Southern Hemisphere is inclined towards it approximately 6 months later.

This changing orientation alters both the angle at which sunlight reaches Earth's surface and the duration for which different locations receive sunlight.

Angle of incidence of sunlight

The solar radiation received by Earth is called insolation, meaning incoming solar radiation.

When the Sun is high above the horizon, its rays strike the surface more directly. The incoming solar energy is concentrated over a relatively small area, resulting in greater energy received per unit area.

When the Sun is low above the horizon, its rays strike the surface obliquely. The same amount of incoming energy is distributed over a larger surface area. Oblique rays also travel through a greater thickness of the atmosphere, increasing the opportunity for scattering and absorption.

Duration of daylight

When a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, most locations in that hemisphere experience longer daylight hours. The Sun also reaches a greater altitude above the horizon at local noon.

Longer daylight combined with more direct sunlight increases the daily solar energy received by the surface. These conditions favour summer.

When a hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, daylight duration decreases and the Sun follows a lower apparent path across the sky. The daily amount of solar energy received decreases, producing winter conditions.

Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres

PeriodNorthern HemisphereSouthern Hemisphere
Around JuneSummerWinter
Around DecemberWinterSummer
Around MarchSpringAutumn
Around SeptemberAutumnSpring

These are conventional astronomical seasons, particularly applicable to temperate latitudes. Tropical regions may experience seasonal conditions more strongly associated with rainfall, such as wet and dry seasons.

For example, December falls during winter in India but during summer in Australia.

Why distance alone cannot explain seasons

Both hemispheres belong to the same planet and are at approximately the same distance from the Sun at any given time. Nevertheless, one hemisphere experiences summer while the other experiences winter.

Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, when the Northern Hemisphere experiences winter. Earth is farthest from the Sun in early July, when the Northern Hemisphere experiences summer.

These observations show that the variation in Earth-Sun distance is not the principal cause of the annual seasonal cycle.

What if Earth had no axial tilt?

If Earth's axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, the overhead Sun would remain near the Equator throughout the year. Most locations would experience little annual variation in daylight duration, and the familiar astronomical seasons caused by axial tilt would largely disappear.

Some variation in solar energy would still occur because Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical.

Prelims focus

  • Axial tilt and annual revolution together produce the seasons.
  • Earth's axis maintains approximately the same orientation during its annual orbit.
  • Summer results from longer daylight and more direct sunlight.
  • The Northern and Southern Hemispheres experience opposite astronomical seasons.
  • Trap: Earth's daily rotation produces day and night, not the annual succession of seasons.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapters 2 and 3, pp. 11-12 and 19-21; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, 2024-25 online reprint, Chapter 8, pp. 67-68; US Naval Observatory, The Seasons and the Earth's Orbit; NASA, What Is Earth?, section on seasons; online references consulted 26 November 2026.]
